```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Synthetic teaching participants; no real patient records.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 80
trial <- data.frame(id = sprintf("P%03d", seq_len(n)),
  arm = factor(rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = n / 2)),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 9)), sbp_0 = rnorm(n, 145, 12))
trial$sbp_12 <- 25 + .8 * trial$sbp_0 + .1 * (trial$age - 60) -
  7 * (trial$arm == "Treatment") + rnorm(n, 0, 7)
trial$response <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-.5 + .8 * (trial$arm == "Treatment") -
                                     .025 * (trial$sbp_0 - 145)))
trial$sbp_0[c(5, 29, 61)] <- NA_real_
```

## The statistical computing sequence {.smaller}

| Session | Question | Main product |
|---|---|---|
| 14 · Simulation | How does a method behave when the truth is known? | A checked simulation study |
| 15 · Resampling | What can repeated use of observed data tell us? | Uncertainty and held-out performance |
| 16 · Practical analysis | How do we fit, inspect, and deliver an analysis? | Models, numerical checks, and an auditable handoff |

This session applies the programming tools from Sessions 11–13 to new statistical tasks.

## What is new today {.smaller}

| Already developed | Today's extension |
|---|---|
| Import, joins, strings, dates (5–7) | Capture structured identifiers and audit rejected records |
| Functions and checks (11–12) | Inspect fitted objects and verify numerical solutions |
| Simulation and resampling (14–15) | Connect fitted models to predictions and computational objectives |
| Projects and Git (1–2) | Record package versions and deliver an analysis bundle |

Basic text cleaning, Git operations, and loop syntax remain prerequisites rather than repeated blocks.

## Learning goals {.smaller}

- Translate a model formula into an analysis dataset and design matrix.
- Extract model results and make predictions on the intended scale.
- Distinguish mean-response intervals, prediction intervals, and held-out error.
- Use one-dimensional optimization, root finding, and integration with checks.
- Parse a narrow identifier grammar while retaining missing and invalid records.
- Preserve the computing environment and provenance of a finished analysis.

## Session outline {.smaller}

| Block | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | A statistical analysis workflow |
| 2 | Formulas and fitted model objects |
| 3 | Prediction and diagnostics |
| 4 | Binary outcomes with `glm()` |
| 5 | Numerical optimization, roots, and integration |
| 6 | Structured text and validation |
| 7 | Reproducible handoff and synthesis |

# 1 · An analysis workflow {.section-divider}

## One synthetic study {.smaller}

```{r}
head(trial[, c("id", "arm", "sbp_0", "sbp_12", "response")], 4)
```

One row represents one participant. Baseline and 12-week SBP are continuous;
`response` is a separately generated binary teaching outcome.

All data are synthetic. The examples teach computing interfaces, not a clinical analysis recommendation.

## Define the target before fitting {.smaller}

| Task | Target | Computing evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Adjusted mean comparison | Model coefficient for treatment at specified covariates | Formula, sample, contrast, interval |
| Predict 12-week SBP | Outcome for a new participant | Predictor availability and held-out error |
| Model a binary response | Probability of `response = 1` | Outcome coding and prediction scale |

These tasks can use similar functions while answering different questions.

## Make the analysis population explicit {.smaller}

```{r}
vars <- c("id", "arm", "sbp_0", "age", "sbp_12", "response")
keep <- complete.cases(trial[, vars])
analysis <- trial[keep, vars]
c(available = nrow(trial), analysed = nrow(analysis), excluded = sum(!keep))
trial$id[!keep]
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(analysis$id))
```

Complete-case filtering is explicit here for teaching. It changes the population
being analysed and may introduce bias; it is not a universal missing-data strategy.

## A checkable analysis contract {.smaller}

- **Input:** one row per participant; specified units and factor levels.
- **Sample:** record exclusions and reasons, retaining identifiers.
- **Fit:** a stated formula and fitting procedure.
- **Output:** estimates or predictions with their target and uncertainty.
- **Evidence:** diagnostic checks, held-out evaluation when relevant, and provenance.

An error-free `lm()` call establishes only that the computation completed.

# 2 · Formulas and model objects {.section-divider}

## Read a model formula {.smaller}

```{r}
f <- sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm
f
```

The response is left of `~`; the terms on the right specify predictors.
An intercept is included by default. In formulas, `+` adds model terms rather
than adding the columns numerically.

Use `data = analysis` so the intended source of variables is clear.

## Formula operators {.smaller}

| Formula fragment | Model terms |
|---|---|
| `x + z` | Main effects of x and z |
| `x * z` | `x + z + x:z` |
| `x:z` | Interaction term |
| `x + I(x^2)` | Linear and literal squared x terms |
| `x - 1` | Remove the intercept |

The formula `^` has special term-expansion meaning. Use `I()` when ordinary
arithmetic is intended. Include interactions because the scientific question
requires them, not simply because the syntax is available.

## Factors determine the comparison {.smaller}

```{r}
analysis$arm <- factor(analysis$arm, levels = c("Control", "Treatment"))
levels(analysis$arm)
contrasts(analysis$arm)
```

With the treatment contrasts used here, Control is the reference.
`armTreatment` represents the Treatment-versus-Control coefficient conditional
on the other terms in this additive model.

Changing the reference changes coefficient interpretation, not the fitted values.

## Inspect the design matrix {.smaller}

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(f, data = analysis)
head(X, 4)
c(rows = nrow(X), columns = ncol(X), rank = qr(X)$rank)
```

Factors become numeric contrast columns. Collinear columns can make coefficients
unidentifiable even when the formula looks reasonable.

## Fit and inspect the object {.smaller}

```{r}
fit <- lm(f, data = analysis, na.action = na.fail)
class(fit)
c(n = nobs(fit), residual_df = df.residual(fit))
coef(fit)
```

`fit` is a structured R object, not the printed coefficient table.
`na.fail` prevents the model from silently dropping additional rows after we
have defined the analysis sample.

## Extract results with model methods {.smaller}

```{r}
coef(summary(fit))
```

| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| `coef(fit)` | Coefficient estimates |
| `confint(fit)` | Model-based coefficient intervals |
| `fitted(fit)` / `residuals(fit)` | Fitted values / residuals |
| `model.frame(fit)` | Variables and rows used for fitting |

Prefer documented methods to copying numbers out of Console output.

## Build a result table {.smaller}

```{r}
ci <- confint(fit)
results <- data.frame(term = names(coef(fit)),
  estimate = unname(coef(fit)), lower = ci[, 1], upper = ci[, 2],
  row.names = NULL)
results
```

State the outcome's units, reference category, sample size, and adjustment terms.
An adjusted coefficient is not automatically a causal effect.

## Verify rows and fitted values {.smaller}

```{r}
stopifnot(nobs(fit) == nrow(analysis),
  nrow(model.frame(fit)) == nrow(analysis),
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(X %*% coef(fit)), as.numeric(fitted(fit)))))
```

This independently checks the link between the matrix, coefficients, and fitted
values. It does not establish that the model assumptions are appropriate.

## Practice: a silent sample change {.smaller}

A report says “80 participants.” The fitted object reports 77 observations.
The analyst used the default missing-value handling in `lm()`.

Which variables and identifiers should be checked? Which denominator belongs
beside the reported coefficient table?

## Practice: inspect the fitted sample {.smaller}

Compare the required variables, the complete-case indicator, `nobs(fit)`, and
`model.frame(fit)`. Record the excluded IDs and the missing fields.

Report the sample actually used by the model. For comparisons between models,
also check whether different formulas cause different rows to be included.

# 3 · Prediction and diagnostics {.section-divider}

## Construct prediction data deliberately {.smaller}

```{r}
new_people <- data.frame(sbp_0 = c(140, 155), age = c(55, 65),
  arm = factor(c("Control", "Treatment"), levels = levels(analysis$arm)))
predict(fit, newdata = new_people)
```

Match predictor names, units, and factor levels. Do not substitute `fitted(fit)`
for predictions on new rows; fitted values describe the training observations.

## Mean-response and prediction intervals {.smaller}

```{r}
mean_ci <- predict(fit, new_people, interval = "confidence")
person_pi <- predict(fit, new_people, interval = "prediction")
round(cbind(mean_ci, prediction_lower = person_pi[, "lwr"],
                     prediction_upper = person_pi[, "upr"]), 2)
```

The confidence interval concerns the conditional **mean** response.
The prediction interval concerns an **individual** future response and also
includes residual variation. Both depend on the model's assumptions.

## Unsupported predictions {.smaller}

- A new factor level may prevent prediction.
- Extrapolation can return a number even far outside the training data.
- A response-derived predictor may be unavailable at deployment.
- A narrow model-based interval does not measure every source of uncertainty.

```{r}
range(analysis$sbp_0)
range(new_people$sbp_0)
```

Inspect prediction inputs before interpreting outputs.

## Residuals versus fitted values {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit), pch = 19, col = "#8a7448",
     xlab = "Fitted 12-week SBP", ylab = "Residual (mmHg)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

Look for curvature, changing spread, and unusual observations. A pattern suggests
follow-up questions; absence of a visible pattern is not proof of adequacy.

## Quantile and influence diagnostics {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(residuals(fit), pch = 19, cex = .6, main = "Residual quantiles")
qqline(residuals(fit))
plot(cooks.distance(fit), type = "h", ylab = "Cook's distance",
     xlab = "Analysis row", main = "Influence")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Investigate flagged records and model sensitivity. Do not delete a participant
only because a diagnostic is large.

## Preserve identifiers in diagnostics {.smaller}

```{r}
diagnostics <- data.frame(id = analysis$id, fitted = fitted(fit),
  residual = residuals(fit), cook = cooks.distance(fit))
head(diagnostics[order(diagnostics$cook, decreasing = TRUE), ], 3)
```

Row numbers can change after filtering or sorting. An ID makes a diagnostic
traceable to its original record.

## Diagnostics and validation differ {.smaller}

| Evidence | Question |
|---|---|
| Residual plots and influence | Where might the fitted model be inadequate or sensitive? |
| Cross-validation from Session 15 | How well does the fitting procedure predict held-out observations? |
| External evaluation | Does performance transfer to the target setting? |

Good training fit is not a substitute for held-out evaluation.

# 4 · Binary outcomes {.section-divider}

## A binomial model in R {.smaller}

```{r}
table(analysis$response)
binary_fit <- glm(response ~ sbp_0 + arm,
  family = binomial(), data = analysis, na.action = na.fail)
coef(binary_fit)
```

Here `response` is numeric 0/1 and the target event is explicitly `response = 1`.
The default binomial link is logit; coefficients are on the log-odds scale.

## Link scale and response scale {.smaller}

```{r}
eta <- predict(binary_fit, newdata = new_people, type = "link")
prob <- predict(binary_fit, newdata = new_people, type = "response")
data.frame(log_odds = eta, probability = prob)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(plogis(eta)), unname(prob))),
          all(prob >= 0 & prob <= 1))
```

Omitting `type` returns link-scale predictions for this GLM. Always label the scale.

## Coefficients and probabilities {.smaller}

```{r}
c(log_odds_coefficient = coef(binary_fit)["armTreatment"],
  conditional_odds_ratio = exp(coef(binary_fit)["armTreatment"]))
```

Exponentiating a logit coefficient gives a conditional odds ratio for that term,
not a risk ratio or probability difference. Predicted probabilities depend on
the other covariates as well.

Statistical interpretation requires the model specification and study design.

## Inspect fitting problems {.smaller}

```{r}
c(converged = binary_fit$converged,
  finite_coefficients = all(is.finite(coef(binary_fit))))
range(fitted(binary_fit))
```

Warnings, very large coefficients, or probabilities near 0 and 1 can require
investigation, including sparse cells or separation. A convergence flag alone
does not establish reliable inference.

Use methods guidance for a remedy; do not suppress warnings until the output looks clean.

# 5 · Numerical computation {.section-divider}

## Three numerical tasks {.smaller}

| Task | R function | Result to check |
|---|---|---|
| Minimize or maximize a scalar function on an interval | `optimize()` | Location, objective, and boundaries |
| Find a zero of a continuous function | `uniroot()` | Root, residual, and bracket |
| Integrate a function over a range | `integrate()` | Value, reported numerical error, and known checks |

Statistical software performs such calculations internally. A transparent
one-dimensional example makes the computational contract visible.

## Write a negative log-likelihood {.smaller}

```{r}
counts <- c(0, 1, 2, 1, 4, 3, 2, 0, 5, 2)
poisson_nll <- function(lambda, y) {
  if (length(lambda) != 1L || !is.finite(lambda) || lambda <= 0)
    return(Inf)
  -sum(dpois(y, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}
poisson_nll(2, counts)
```

For independent Poisson counts, log-probabilities add. The negative sign makes
maximum likelihood a minimization problem. These counts share the same exposure.

## Inspect the objective {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.7
grid <- seq(.1, 6, length.out = 150)
plot(grid, vapply(grid, poisson_nll, numeric(1), y = counts), type = "l",
     xlab = "Poisson mean", ylab = "Negative log-likelihood", lwd = 2)
abline(v = mean(counts), lty = 2, col = "#8a7448")
```

A plot can reveal a wrong sign, a poor search interval, or multiple minima.
It complements numerical checks; it does not prove the global solution.

## Optimize and verify a known answer {.smaller}

```{r}
opt <- optimize(poisson_nll, interval = c(.001, 10), y = counts)
c(numerical = opt$minimum, analytic = mean(counts), objective = opt$objective)
stopifnot(abs(opt$minimum - mean(counts)) < 1e-3)
```

For these Poisson observations, the maximum-likelihood mean is the sample mean.
Agreement checks this implementation against a result available independently.

## Boundaries and tolerances {.smaller}

```{r}
narrow <- optimize(poisson_nll, interval = c(.001, 1), y = counts)
c(wrong_search_result = narrow$minimum, known_solution = mean(counts))
```

The algorithm searches the interval supplied. A result near a boundary requires
checking the interval and the parameter space.

If every count is zero, the Poisson optimum is the boundary `lambda = 0`;
the positive-only objective above needs a separate boundary rule.

## Root finding as an inverse calculation {.smaller}

```{r}
target <- function(z) pnorm(z) - .975
c(left = target(0), right = target(4))
root <- uniroot(target, interval = c(0, 4), tol = 1e-8)
c(root = root$root, residual = target(root$root), reference = qnorm(.975))
```

For a continuous function, opposite endpoint signs bracket at least one root.
Check the equation at the returned value, not only the convergence message.

## Numerical integration {.smaller}

```{r}
area <- integrate(dnorm, lower = -1.96, upper = 1.96)
c(numerical = area$value, reported_error = area$abs.error,
  cdf_difference = pnorm(1.96) - pnorm(-1.96))
```

The integrand must accept a vector of inputs and return corresponding values.
The reported error concerns numerical approximation, not sampling uncertainty.

## Practice: classify the failure {.smaller}

1. A likelihood optimizer returns the upper limit of a narrow search interval.
2. A root finder receives endpoints where the function has the same sign.
3. Increasing simulation replicates does not change a mistaken likelihood formula.

For each, identify what should be inspected before increasing iteration limits.

## Practice: check the mathematical contract {.smaller}

1. Plot the objective, inspect the parameter space, and expand a justified interval.
2. Check continuity, the equation, and a bracket containing a sign change.
3. Validate the formula against a known case; more repetition cannot repair it.

Numerical tolerance, Monte Carlo error, and sampling uncertainty describe different problems.

# 6 · Structured text {.section-divider}

## A narrow identifier grammar {.smaller}

```{r}
specimen_raw <- c(" P001-W00 ", "P010-W12", "P020-W99", "P999-W04",
                  "junkP003-W12", "P004-W4", NA, "P005-W12")
specimen_raw
```

The specification is `P` + three digits + `-W` + two digits.
Permitted visits are 0, 4, 12, and 26, and the participant must exist in the registry.

Shape, allowed values, and registry membership are separate checks.

## Anchors and capture groups {.smaller}

```{r}
pattern <- "^(P[0-9]{3})-W([0-9]{2})$"
normalized <- toupper(trimws(specimen_raw))
stringr::str_match(normalized, pattern)
```

`^` and `$` require the complete string to match. Parentheses capture the
participant ID and visit. The returned matrix preserves one row per input,
including missing values and nonmatches.

## Escaping and literal punctuation {.smaller}

```{r}
x <- c("report.csv", "reportXcsv")
data.frame(x, loose = grepl(".csv$", x),
  literal_dot = grepl("\\.csv$", x),
  raw_string = grepl(r"(\.csv$)", x))
```

R string parsing and regex parsing are separate layers. A raw string removes
R's backslash doubling; it does not remove the regex engine's special syntax.
Use literal matching when no pattern language is needed.

## Preserve rows in base R extraction {.smaller}

```{r}
parts <- regmatches(normalized, regexec(pattern, normalized))
id_base <- vapply(parts, function(z)
  if (length(z) == 3L) z[2] else NA_character_, character(1))
id_stringr <- stringr::str_match(normalized, pattern)[, 2]
stopifnot(identical(unname(id_base), unname(id_stringr)))
```

A failed match is retained as missing. Do not drop nonmatches and then attach
the shorter result to the original data by position.

## An auditable parser {.smaller}

```{r}
parse_specimen <- function(x, known_ids) {
  stopifnot(is.character(x), is.character(known_ids))
  clean <- toupper(trimws(x))
  m <- stringr::str_match(clean, "^(P[0-9]{3})-W([0-9]{2})$")
  id <- m[, 2]; week <- as.integer(m[, 3])
  status <- ifelse(is.na(x), "missing", ifelse(is.na(id), "bad format",
    ifelse(!id %in% known_ids, "unknown ID",
      ifelse(!week %in% c(0L, 4L, 12L, 26L), "invalid visit", "ok"))))
  data.frame(raw = x, normalized = clean, id, week, status)
}
```

The first failing rule supplies `status`; the raw value remains available for review.

## Test near misses and semantic failures {.smaller}

```{r}
parsed <- parse_specimen(specimen_raw, trial$id)
expected <- c("ok", "ok", "invalid visit", "unknown ID",
              "bad format", "bad format", "missing", "ok")
stopifnot(nrow(parsed) == length(specimen_raw),
          identical(parsed$status, expected))
parsed[, c("raw", "id", "week", "status")]
```

`P020-W99` has the right shape but an invalid visit. A regex alone cannot verify
the study protocol or registry membership.

## Review before joining {.smaller}

```{r}
table(parsed$status, useNA = "ifany")
accepted <- parsed[parsed$status == "ok", ]
review <- parsed[parsed$status != "ok", ]
stopifnot(nrow(accepted) + nrow(review) == nrow(parsed))
```

Check uniqueness of the intended key before joining. Multiple specimens at the
same participant-visit may be legitimate; determine whether a specimen ID is also needed.

## Keep pattern matching within its scope {.smaller}

- A valid-looking identifier is not evidence of a valid study record.
- A text mention is not equivalent to a confirmed condition or medication use.
- Clinical negation and ambiguous instructions need domain-aware review.
- Date strings need date parsing and calendar validation, already introduced earlier.

Use a documented grammar for structured text. Keep uncertain records visible.

# 7 · Reproducible handoff {.section-divider}

## Record what produced the result {.smaller}

```{r}
analysis_bundle <- list(
  formula = formula(fit), analysed_ids = analysis$id,
  excluded_ids = trial$id[!keep], coefficients = results,
  seed = 6301, rng = RNGkind(), session = sessionInfo())
names(analysis_bundle)
```

Also record the input version, analysis-code revision, and missing-data policy.
In this teaching example the generator and seed define the synthetic input.

## Save objects and plain tables {.smaller}

```r
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(analysis_bundle, "output/analysis-bundle.rds")
write.csv(results, "output/coefficients.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(review, "output/specimen-review.csv", row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "output/session-info.txt")
```

RDS preserves R structure; CSV supports inspection in other tools.
The report explains the result. The source and input specification make it reproducible.

## Package versions are part of the environment {.smaller}

`sessionInfo()` records the active R session but does not recreate its packages.
`renv` adds a project library and a lockfile describing package dependencies.

```r
# Optional: run interactively in a dedicated project, not during report rendering.
renv::init()
# After confirming the project works:
renv::snapshot()
# In a clone with the committed lockfile:
renv::restore()
```

These commands are a setup workflow, not required execution in today's lab.

## What to version and what to document {.smaller}

| Keep in project history | Document separately |
|---|---|
| Analysis source and input specification | Data access and permitted storage |
| `renv.lock`, activation files, and settings | Required R version and system dependencies |
| Tests and a concise README | How to regenerate expensive results |

Follow renv's generated ignore rules; do not commit its installed package library.
A lockfile records dependencies, not the data, operating system, or complete machine.

## A reproducible delivery check {.smaller}

1. Open a clean R session in the documented project environment.
2. Obtain the specified input and run the analysis from the documented entry point.
3. Confirm sample counts, key uniqueness, coefficient names, and prediction checks.
4. Render the report and inspect tables and figures.
5. Confirm that the outputs identify their input, code, and environment versions.

Use a colleague's rerun to test the instructions, not only your current workspace.

## Integrated lab {.smaller}

| Task | Evidence to produce |
|---|---|
| Fit and inspect an adjusted model | Analysis counts, coefficient table, and diagnostics |
| Predict continuous and binary outcomes | Correct scales, intervals, and input checks |
| Verify numerical calculations | Known-answer comparisons and boundary discussion |
| Parse structured specimen IDs | Field tests and a review queue |
| Prepare the handoff | Saved outputs and an environment record |

Each task uses an interface introduced in the corresponding lecture block.

## Course synthesis {.smaller}

| Earlier work | Evidence in a finished analysis |
|---|---|
| Workflow and version control | A rerunnable project with identifiable inputs and code |
| Data handling and visualization | A checked analysis population and interpretable figures |
| Programming and debugging | Functions with explicit contracts and meaningful checks |
| Simulation and resampling | Uncertainty and performance evaluated against the right target |
| Today's practical tools | Inspectable models, verified numerical results, and traceable outputs |

## Exit check {.smaller}

Explain each discrepancy before accepting the result:

- The model sample is smaller than the report's denominator.
- A binomial prediction is negative because it is on the link scale.
- An optimizer returns a boundary because the interval excludes the solution.
- A specimen ID matches the pattern but is absent from the registry.
- The report runs locally but its package environment is undocumented.

- [R GLM prediction scales](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/predict.glm.html)

## Summary {.smaller}

Specify the target and sample, inspect the fitted object, and label prediction
scales. Check numerical results against the equation or a known answer. Preserve
uncertain text records and document the environment behind the final outputs.
